query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction (~5 at%) of a ductilizing element such as vanadium (V) into the NbMoTaW high-entropy alloy (HEA) will improve its room-temperature ductility by promoting dislocation mobility, without significantly compromising its high-temperature mechanical strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Alloying NbMoTaW with ~5 at% vanadium (V), forming NbMoTaWV0.05
generation.conditions: Room temperature, 1600 °C, and under irradiation (e.g., ion or neutron irradiation)
generation.structural_mediator: BCC lattice with increased lattice distortion and local chemical complexity due to V addition
generation.mechanism: Vanadium addition reduces the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion in BCC HEAs, facilitating dislocation glide at room temperature. The small addition maintains the single-phase BCC structure and high configurational entropy, preserving high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: NbMoTaWV0.05 will exhibit higher room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased elongation to failure or reduction in brittle fracture) compared to baseline NbMoTaW, while retaining comparable mechanical strength at 1600 °C and similar irradiation resistance (e.g., defect accumulation and swelling).
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy, which is brittle at room temperature but strong at 1600 °C and predicted to be irradiation resistant.
generation.boundary: Vanadium addition must remain low (<10 at%) to avoid phase separation or excessive softening; the alloy must remain single-phase BCC.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of ductility improvement and potential trade-offs in high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance are uncertain due to lack of direct experimental evidence for NbMoTaWV alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare NbMoTaWV0.05 and baseline NbMoTaW alloys by arc melting. Characterize phase structure by XRD and SEM. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1600 °C. Subject samples to ion irradiation and measure defect density and swelling.
measurements: Defect density and swelling after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If NbMoTaWV0.05 does not show improved room-temperature ductility relative to NbMoTaW, or if its high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance is significantly degraded, the hypothesis is falsified.
